chapter_theme: Destruction (அழித்தல்): the Lord burns the world, the sea and the asuras with fire as his arrow, and the worlds are consumed like rice in the pot. Yet dissolution is also inward and saving: four kinds of saṃhāra run from daily sleep to the dissolution that is the truth of grace, and what returns to the void leaves the void itself unharmed.
structure_note: Cosmic burning (421 to 424) gives way to four verses (425 to 428) that each name the same four dissolutions (நித்த, வைத்த, சுத்த, உய்த்த) but define them differently, then to the image of crop and waste ground (429) and the Lord who destroys deeds (430).

421.reading: The Lord who made fire burned the wide world, burned the surging sea, burned the asuras; fire is that Lord's arrow in hand.
421.nuance: Burning the asuras recalls the burning of the three cities, where the arrow is usually Vishnu with fire at its tip; here fire is the whole arrow. அங்கிசெய்து may also be 'wielding fire'.

422.reading: In the three dissolutions I came to know that the order which stood as one aeon was undone; the world, like soft rice on the boil, and the great land the mountains bore were burnt.
422.nuance: இலயங்கள் மூன்று and ஒன்றுகற்பாந்த are technical and not fixed by the verse. The image is plain: the world softens and is consumed like rice in the pot.

423.reading: The earth that gives footing, the eight snowy mountains, the seven seas with their tides and all the rest, the fire takes hold of and burns, and space too; there is no wonder in the heart that knows it.
423.nuance: பதஞ்செய்யும், உதஞ்செய்யும், குதஞ்செய்யும், விதஞ்செய்யும் rhyme but are hard to gloss; குதம் may be 'destroying' and விதம் 'forms'. The last line may mean the wise are not astonished at the world's end.

424.reading: The noble stream that came down from the cloud mountain, seeping through the cosmos to the eight directions, he set as fire upon the pit beyond Om.
424.nuance: குலக்கொடி may be the Ganga or a power such as kundalini; குண்டம் is the fire pit of the rite. The verse seems to make cosmic burning a fire rite beyond the syllable Om, but every term here is open.

425.reading: Daily dissolution is sleep's long stupor; the held dissolution is the state beyond waking; pure dissolution is kevala where action ceases; the dissolution that lifts up is the truth of the Supreme's grace.
425.nuance: The four names (நித்த, வைத்த, சுத்த, உய்த்த சங்காரம்) are technical. கேவலம் in Siddhanta usually names the soul's state wholly under anava, which sits oddly with 'pure'. Only the last term is constant across 425 to 428: the highest dissolution is grace.

426.reading: Daily dissolution is the putting off of the two bodies; the held dissolution is the dissolution of Maya; pure dissolution is immersion beyond the mind; the dissolution that lifts up is the truth of Siva's grace.
426.nuance: இரண்டுடல் (two bodies) may be the gross and subtle bodies. The same names as 425 receive different definitions.

427.reading: Daily dissolution is when the instruments' troubles are removed; the matching dissolution is shedding body and life; pure dissolution is immersion in what is beyond; the dissolution that lifts up is the truth of the Supreme's grace.
427.nuance: ஒத்த stands where 425 and 426 have வைத்த; the variant line வைத்தசங் காரங் கேவலம் ஆன்மாவுக் restores வைத்த and ties it to kevala. கருவி (instruments) are the faculties.

428.reading: Daily dissolution is in relieving long weariness; held dissolution is in the abiding beginningless bond; pure dissolution is the Supreme's untouched grace; and there is the dissolution that lifts up, when the four are weighed.
428.nuance: அனாதி (beginningless) is commonly taken as anava, the beginningless impurity. நாலா மதிக்கிலே closes the series by asking that the four be weighed together.

429.reading: The crop that rises with waste ground as its source, though it sinks back into waste, does not make the old waste waste away; the doings of Mal and Ayan, in the dissolution that does not last, sink as crop of the waste back into that waste.
429.nuance: பாழ் is barren ground and also the void; the verse plays on it six times. The plain sense is a field: what grows from it returns to it while the ground endures. Taken symbolically, the source (Maya or the void) outlasts what it yields, and even Vishnu's and Brahma's works end there.

430.reading: There is one strong Lord who set the deeds that reach evildoers to perish; he gave a body, mingled everywhere, set a company that thinks, and set those who understand.
430.nuance: மாயவைத்தான் may be 'made to perish' or 'set in Maya', and the reading turns on it. On the first reading, destruction here is the destruction of bad karma, a mercy, not a punishment. ஆயம் recalls 407.

links.note: Both put the world in the pot on the fire (உலை). The Naladiyar's turtle plays in the water not knowing it is being cooked, as men revel while Death waits; Tirumular sees the whole world softened and burnt like rice, a cosmic act he says he has come to know, not a warning to the heedless.
The same four names of dissolution, defined differently: daily dissolution is sleep's stupor in 425 and shedding the two bodies in 426. Only the last, grace, stays fixed across 425 to 428.

source_issues: 425 to 428 give four differing definitions of the same four dissolutions; they may be variant recensions of one verse kept side by side.
427: line 2 has ஒத்தசங் காரம் where the parallel verses have வைத்த; the variant வைத்தசங் காரங் கேவலம் ஆன்மாவுக் restores it.
427: line 3 is printed with a stray space (டோ ய்வுறல்) for டோய்வுறல்.
430: line 1 reads தீயவைத் தார்மிங்கள், apparently a misprint (perhaps தீயவைத் தார்தங்கள்).
